title: The Problem Is the Pace
paragraphs: Debates about climate change often treat carbon dioxide as a newcomer, yet the gas is a natural part of the atmosphere, released by volcanoes and living organisms long before humans existed. What has changed is the scale. Understanding that history helps separate natural variation from human influence. According to NASA, industrial activity has raised the concentration of atmospheric carbon dioxide by nearly fifty percent since seventeen fifty, mainly through the burning of fossil fuels and the clearing of forests.

Knowing this requires a way of measuring the past. Ice cores drilled in Greenland, Antarctica and tropical glaciers trap tiny bubbles of ancient air, and when those bubbles are analysed they reveal past concentrations of greenhouse gases. Compared with recent direct measurements, they show the climate responding to changes in those gases. Layer by layer, the ice preserves a record that stretches back far beyond written history.

The decisive contrast is one of speed. NASA reports that carbon dioxide from human activities is now increasing roughly two hundred and fifty times faster than it did from natural sources after the last ice age. Ecosystems and societies can adapt to slow change, but rapid change shortens the time available for adjustment. That is why the argument is less about the existence of a greenhouse effect, which is natural and essential, than about the pace at which we are altering it. Slowing the rise is therefore a question of timing as much as of intention. Facing that reality calmly is the first step towards sensible choices.
